candidates.attacker_control: perfectoConnectLocation, perfectoConnectFile and pcParameters are attacker-influenced if the adversary can create or edit a job using the Perfecto Connect build wrapper (Item/Configure) or inject values into its persisted configuration (Job DSL/seed jobs, config-as-code pipelines, imported job config.xml). cloudName and apiKey are attacker-influenced if the adversary can create or modify a PerfectoCredentials entry referenced by a configured job (credential-store write, including folder-scoped credential creation by less-privileged users). The descriptor helpers doCheckPerfectoConnectLocation and doCheckPerfectoConnectFile only reject empty values (lines 378-381 and 391-394), do not sanitize metacharacters, and skip all checks when the ancestor Item resolves to null (lines 373-375 and 386-388). No validation exists for the credential-sourced cloudName or apiKey.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified in source: (1) @POST and Jenkins.get().checkPermission(Jenkins.ADMINISTER) are present in doFillCredentialIdItems and doCheckCredentialId (lines 332-334 and 358-360) and item.checkPermission(Item.CONFIGURE) in the location and file checks (lines 376 and 389), so the older unauthenticated CSRF/permission gaps are already fixed and are not the finding; (2) token masking on line 161 shows intent to avoid logging the secret, so the residual exposure is via argv rather than the log; (3) the ^[A-Za-z0-9-]+$ filter at line 174 constrains only the parsed tunnel ID, not the command construction; (4) Jenkins threat model generally treats Item/Configure as trusted (such a user could add a shell build step anyway), which lowers severity for the configuration-field vector, while the credential-derived and imported/templated configuration vectors carry the stronger privilege-crossing argument. No runtime testing, build, or dependency verification was performed; conclusions are from source text only.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary operating-system command execution in the process context of the Jenkins controller or agent running the build (compromise of that host Jenkins identity, and of Jenkins itself when the wrapper runs on the controller), reachable by simply starting a build that uses the wrapper. Secondarily, the live Perfecto security token and cloud name are placed in the child process argument vector, so any local user, co-tenant build, or process monitor on the same machine can read the secret from ps output or /proc/<pid>/cmdline; because the token is interpolated unquoted, a secret containing shell metacharacters also changes the command meaning. Partial hardening exists: line 161 logs the equivalent command with the token replaced by a masked placeholder, but the real token is still passed on the actual command line.
candidates.prerequisites: A job must use the Perfecto Connect build wrapper (or otherwise reference a Perfecto credential) and a build must run the wrapper setUp, which happens unconditionally because the configured RunCondition condition field is never evaluated in setUp. Injected commands execute with the privileges of the Jenkins controller or agent process whose JVM runs the wrapper (the same account that launches the Perfecto Connect client).
candidates.root_cause: PerfectoBuildWrapper.getTunnelId builds a command line by direct string concatenation of configuration and credential values and executes it through a shell without quoting, escaping, or validation. pcLocation is built from the data-bound perfectoConnectLocation and perfectoConnectFile fields (lines 155-159); baseCommand interpolates cloudName and the decrypted security token from credentials.getPassword().getPlainText() (lines 160 and 218); pcParameters is appended unquoted. On Windows the whole string becomes a single cmd.exe /c argument (lines 163-164); on Unix it becomes the single bash -c script text, including the raw perfectoConnectLocation inserted after cd (lines 166-167).
candidates.title: Unescaped shell command construction in getTunnelId permits OS command injection and exposes the Perfecto security token as a process argument
candidates.trace: Job configuration (data-bound form) -> @DataBoundConstructor stores perfectoConnectLocation/perfectoConnectFile/pcParameters (lines 130-149; fields at 84, 93, 108) -> persisted in the job config.xml -> setUp (line 205) resolves credentials = PerfectoCredentials.getPerfectoCredentials(build, this) (line 209) and decrypts the token with credentials.getPassword().getPlainText() (line 218) -> getTunnelId(perfectoConnectLocation, credentials.getCloudName(), apiKey, listener) (line 219) -> pcLocation concatenation (lines 155-159) -> baseCommand (line 160) -> Windows: cmd.exe /c with baseCommand plus pcParameters (lines 163-164), or Unix: bash -c with cd, baseCommand and pcParameters concatenated (line 166) -> new ProcessBuilder(...).start() and Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...) (lines 164 and 167). The P1 index independently flags the process-spawning calls at lines 164 and 167 and the setUp -> getTunnelId call edge at line 219.
candidates.unverified: The practical exploitability threshold depends on the deployment permission model (who may configure jobs and who may create Perfecto credentials), which this snapshot does not reveal. The credential resolution code (PerfectoCredentials.getPerfectoCredentials, getCloudName, getPassword/getApiKey) resides in files excluded from this review by the sensitive-path filter, so its permission checks and exact secret field could not be inspected. The bash and cmd.exe execution paths were not executed and the Perfecto Connect client output behaviour was not observed.
candidates.weakness_type: OS Command Injection (CWE-78); sensitive information in process arguments (CWE-214/CWE-522)

coverage_summary: Reviewed all 13 model-visible files of the assigned snapshot: both Java sources in full (PerfectoBuildWrapper.java lines 1-462 and PerfectoEnvironmentUtil.java lines 1-61), pom.xml (version 1.17, dependency and build model inspected), README.md, .gitignore, and the seven help HTML resources. Process-execution sinks, permission guards, credential handling and validation paths were examined in source text; the P1 relation index was used only for navigation (symbol, call and containment candidates, including the setUp -> getTunnelId call edge and process-call hints at lines 164 and 167) and each candidate was re-verified against source. Five of eighteen source-root files are excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter and were unreadable, most importantly the io/plugins/perfecto/credentials package containing PerfectoCredentials, getPerfectoCredentials, migrateToCredentials and the secret accessor. The index parsed only the two Java files (13 indexed, 5 missing, 124 unresolved calls, no control-flow or data-flow analysis). src/test contains no files, and no build, test, scanner or execution was performed.
limitations: Five of eighteen source files are excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter and could not be read; the credential lookup, credential class and migration code invoked from the reviewed file are unverified, so a permission or storage flaw inside them would have been missed.

The P1 relation index has partial coverage (13 of 18 files indexed, only 2 Java files parsed), lacks control-flow and data-flow analysis, reports 124 unresolved calls, and its annotation handling is name-based only; all index facts were treated as navigation hints and re-checked in source.

No dynamic verification was performed (no build, tests, scanner or payload execution), so runtime reachability of the command construction and the behaviour of the Perfecto Connect client are inferred from source alone.

Severity of the candidate depends on Jenkins permission configuration (who holds Item/Configure, who may create Perfecto credentials) and on whether wrapper configuration can be influenced by imported or templated job definitions, none of which is determinable from this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Secret disclosure through the build log
rejected_leads.reason: Line 161 deliberately prints the command with a masked token placeholder, and no readable code path prints the plaintext token; the residual exposure is via process arguments and is folded into the main candidate rather than counted separately.

rejected_leads.lead: Inconsistent secret accessors getPassword() in setUp (line 218) versus getApiKey() in migrateCredentials (lines 412 and 427)
rejected_leads.reason: PerfectoCredentials is unreadable in this run (excluded path), so no security consequence can be established for this possible functional or library-version bug.

rejected_leads.lead: PerfectoCredentials object persisted as a non-transient wrapper field (line 97, assigned at line 209)
rejected_leads.reason: Because the wrapper is XStream-serialized into the job config.xml, the credential object may be re-serialized into job configuration on the next save, duplicating the secret outside the credential store and leaving it behind after rotation; however it cannot be verified whether its persisted fields include a Secret or plaintext value, and Jenkins encrypts Secret values with the controller master key. Unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing permission check when the ancestor Item is null in doCheckPerfectoConnectLocation and doCheckPerfectoConnectFile (lines 373-375 and 386-388)
rejected_leads.reason: These endpoints only report whether a value is empty and disclose no protected data or state, so no concrete security impact was identified.

rejected_leads.lead: Credential lookup performed with ACL.SYSTEM (lines 347 and 365)
rejected_leads.reason: Both call sites are gated by Jenkins.get().checkPermission(Jenkins.ADMINISTER) beforehand (lines 334 and 360), so no lower-privileged credential enumeration path is demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Null-pointer failures at line 142 (tunnelIdCustomName.length) and lines 212/217 (reuseTunnelId.contains) for missing legacy fields
rejected_leads.reason: Availability and robustness defect rather than an attacker-controlled security vulnerability; no evidence of a remote trigger by an unprivileged user.

rejected_leads.lead: Configured RunCondition never evaluated in setUp (field at line 100) and environment variable name taken from job config with overwrite=true (line 234)
rejected_leads.reason: Both require job-configuration control that already implies broader capabilities; behaviour is logic and robustness oriented, and the tunnel-ID value is constrained by the ^[A-Za-z0-9-]+$ filter at line 174.

summary: The repository is the Jenkins Perfecto plugin (pom.xml version 1.17) with two readable Java sources: PerfectoBuildWrapper (build wrapper and descriptor) and PerfectoEnvironmentUtil (environment-variable helper). The strongest source-evidenced issue is in the tunnel-start path: getTunnelId concatenates job-configuration fields (perfectoConnectLocation, perfectoConnectFile, pcParameters) plus stored-credential values (cloudName and the decrypted security token apiKey via Secret.getPlainText) into a shell command string that is handed verbatim to cmd.exe /c on Windows (lines 163-164) and to bash -c on Unix (lines 166-167), with no quoting, escaping or allow-list validation. The only validators on those fields (lines 372-395) merely reject empty values, and the credential fields are never validated. A path or additional parameter containing shell metacharacters such as ;, &&, $(...), backticks, quotes, or Windows & | %VAR% is therefore interpreted as shell syntax and executes arbitrary commands in the Jenkins process context during setUp. The same construction places the live Perfecto security token in the child process argument vector (line 160), where it is readable via ps or /proc/<pid>/cmdline by other local users or co-tenant builds, even though the plugin masks the token when logging the equivalent command (line 161). This is an unverified lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability; practical severity depends on who can influence the wrapper configuration or a referenced credential, since Jenkins normally treats Item/Configure as a trusted permission.
